claims.claim: Töyrylä notes the Ettocio scene describes Alessan, Devin and the disguised Sandre without naming them, so readers half-recognise what the focalizant cannot.
claims.source: Roosa Töyrylä, 'Ambiguities and Divided Loyalties: Focalization in Guy Gavriel Kay's Tigana' (BA thesis, University of Helsinki, 2017)
claims.quote: readers are not directly told who the characters are

claims.claim: Webb notes Tigana's magic correlates with psychological strength and the text contains no talismanic objects, staffs or reforged swords.
claims.source: Janeen Webb, 'Myth and the New High Fantasy: Guy Gavriel Kay's Tigana', The Ring Bearer 8.2 (Spring 1991)
claims.quote: the text contains no talismanic objects

claims.claim: Webb describes three major narrative strands plaited toward one outcome whose players never see the whole; the gods and the reader do.
claims.source: Janeen Webb, 'Myth and the New High Fantasy: Guy Gavriel Kay's Tigana', The Ring Bearer 8.2 (Spring 1991)
claims.quote: The gods, and the reader, may see the whole tapestry

claims.claim: Webb observes that decisive freely-willed acts are timed to the Ember Days, which interweaves the separate strands.
claims.source: Janeen Webb, 'Myth and the New High Fantasy: Guy Gavriel Kay's Tigana', The Ring Bearer 8.2 (Spring 1991)
claims.quote: It is this timing that helps to interweave the narrative strands

claims.claim: Webb reads Rhun as a deliberate pun on 'ruin' and a Welsh reference, naming being crucial to the text.
claims.source: Janeen Webb, 'Myth and the New High Fantasy: Guy Gavriel Kay's Tigana', The Ring Bearer 8.2 (Spring 1991)

claims.claim: Webb notes Tigana ends with a riselka whose presence is a prophecy in itself.
claims.source: Janeen Webb, 'Myth and the New High Fantasy: Guy Gavriel Kay's Tigana', The Ring Bearer 8.2 (Spring 1991)
claims.quote: whose presence is a prophecy in itself

claims.claim: Webb argues Kay keeps, line by line, the sentence structure, ambience and style of nineteenth-century romance while repudiating its cosy certainties.
claims.source: Janeen Webb, 'Post-Romantic Romance: Guy Gavriel Kay's Tigana and A Song for Arbonne', New York Review of Science Fiction 77 (Jan 1995)
claims.quote: the sentence structure, the ambience, the style of nineteenth century romance

claims.claim: Webb traces a progression from Homeric gods (Fionavar) to intercessory gods (Tigana) to off-stage gods and engineered miracles (Arbonne).
claims.source: Janeen Webb, 'Post-Romantic Romance: Guy Gavriel Kay's Tigana and A Song for Arbonne', New York Review of Science Fiction 77 (Jan 1995)
claims.quote: a clear progression from myth through faith to religion

claims.claim: Webb calls A Song for Arbonne a meta-fantasy bred from nineteenth-century historical romance crossed with late-twentieth-century cynicism.
claims.source: Janeen Webb, 'Post-Romantic Romance: Guy Gavriel Kay's Tigana and A Song for Arbonne', New York Review of Science Fiction 77 (Jan 1995)
claims.quote: bred from the root stock of nineteenth century historical romance

claims.claim: Webb sees Bertran de Talair as reminiscent of Dunnett's Francis Crawford of Lymond, musician and strategist.
claims.source: Janeen Webb, 'Post-Romantic Romance: Guy Gavriel Kay's Tigana and A Song for Arbonne', New York Review of Science Fiction 77 (Jan 1995)
claims.quote: reminiscent of Dunnett’s Francis Crawford of Lymond

claims.claim: Webb notes a colour symbolism of darkness and light in the female characters carried from Tigana into Arbonne.
claims.source: Janeen Webb, 'Post-Romantic Romance: Guy Gavriel Kay's Tigana and A Song for Arbonne', New York Review of Science Fiction 77 (Jan 1995)
claims.quote: The colour symbolism of darkness and light has been retained

claims.claim: Webb's essay carries an appended 'GGK NOTE' in which Kay disputes her reading of Arbonne's gender balance, a rare author–critic exchange in the record.
claims.source: Janeen Webb, 'Post-Romantic Romance: Guy Gavriel Kay's Tigana and A Song for Arbonne', New York Review of Science Fiction 77 (Jan 1995)
claims.quote: Janeen Webb takes the unusual and generous step

claims.claim: Ordway shows Kay converting the Cid's beard-pulling into a whip-scar because the scarring impresses a modern reader.
claims.source: Holly E. Ordway, 'The World-Building of Guy Gavriel Kay' (UMass Amherst independent study, 1998; presented at the 1998 Academic Conference on Canadian SF&F)
claims.quote: unlikely to impress a modern reader, whereas the scarring does

claims.claim: Ordway argues the twenty-year reconquest lets the reader experience victory through characters tied to both sides, so complexities are brought home rather than stated in an epilogue.
claims.source: Holly E. Ordway, 'The World-Building of Guy Gavriel Kay' (UMass Amherst independent study, 1998; presented at the 1998 Academic Conference on Canadian SF&F)
claims.quote: the complexities of the reconquest are brought home

claims.claim: Ordway contrasts Fionavar's many myths with the standalone novels' focus on a single source each.
claims.source: Holly E. Ordway, 'The World-Building of Guy Gavriel Kay' (UMass Amherst independent study, 1998; presented at the 1998 Academic Conference on Canadian SF&F)
claims.quote: he focuses on a single source for each novel

verdicts.trueWording: readers are not directly told who the characters are
verdicts.note: Live fetch (HTTP 200, browser UA). Quote exact. Page names all three: Alessan (recognisable from 'grey-eyed merchant'), Devin ('[t]he young fellow leaning on the bar'), and Duke Sandre disguised as a Khardhu warrior with body-paint, 'likely to go unnoticed'; and states 'readers, unlike Ettocio, are probably able to sense that there is something curious about the scene ... but not to realize the full truth' — the half-recognition limb. Byline confirms Roosa Toyryla, BA thesis, University of Helsinki, 2017.

verdicts.trueWording: the text contains no talismanic objects, staffs of power, or reforged swords
verdicts.note: Live fetch (HTTP 200). Quote exact. Preceding clause supplies the other limb verbatim: 'The magic depicted in this book exists in direct correlation with the psychological strength of those who are able to harness it'. Header confirms Janeen Webb, The Ring Bearer vol 8 no 2, Spring 1991.

verdicts.trueWording: three major strands of action, plaited into the tale ... towards a single outcome
verdicts.note: Live fetch (HTTP 200). Quote exact ('The gods, and the reader, may see the whole tapestry-the players do not'). Every limb present: 'There are three major strands of action, plaited into the tale - the storylines cross ... always being woven towards a single outcome', and the players' ignorance is instanced by Dianora and by Alessan never learning Rhun was Valentin.

verdicts.trueWording: freely willed actions performed by the protagonists on the relevant Ember Days
verdicts.note: Live fetch (HTTP 200). Quote exact. Immediately preceded by 'the major events have their genesis in the emphatically freely willed actions performed by the protagonists on the relevant Ember Days', then illustrated by Dianora saving Brandin on the first Ember day of Spring while Baerd fights for the Night Walkers.

verdicts.trueWording: Naming is crucial to this text ... a deliberate pun on ruin
verdicts.note: Live fetch (HTTP 200). All three limbs verbatim: 'Naming is crucial to this text, and Brandin has named his Fool Rhun-a deliberate pun on ruin'; and separately 'The name Rhun is a direct reference to the Welsh story related by the first Taliesan (Gwion) of the High King Rhun's campaign against the men of the North'.

verdicts.trueWording: see a riselka, whose presence is a prophecy in itself
verdicts.note: Live fetch (HTTP 200). Quote exact, in the essay's closing sentence: 'It ends, intriguingly, with a creature from the book's own mythology, when the wizard Sandre, the archer Baerd, and the musician Devin see a riselka, whose presence is a prophecy in itself', followed by the three-men-see-a-riselka verse.

verdicts.trueWording: line by line, he maintains the sentence structure, the ambience, the style
verdicts.note: Live fetch (HTTP 200). Quote exact and both limbs in one sentence: 'line by line, he maintains the sentence structure, the ambience, the style of nineteenth century romance, yet he repudiates the cosy certainties and overt patterning of much current fantasy'. Header confirms NYRSF No.77, January 1995.

verdicts.trueWording: a clear progression from myth through faith to religion
verdicts.note: Live fetch (HTTP 200). Quote exact; the three stages follow verbatim: 'In mythic Fionavar ... Homeric interaction between gods and mortals'; in Tigana the gods 'may occasionally intercede for their worshippers'; in Arbonne 'the gods remain completely off stage' and the goddess's arrow was 'the product of a little pre-emptive religious engineering by Beatritz' — the engineered-miracle limb.

verdicts.trueWording: a meta-fantasy bred from the root stock of nineteenth century historical romance
verdicts.note: Live fetch (HTTP 200). Quote exact in the essay's opening sentence, with the remaining limb attached: 'and crossed with late twentieth century cynicism about the politics of art, sexuality, and religion'.

verdicts.trueWording: whom Bertran resembles ... as musician and military strategist
verdicts.note: Live fetch (HTTP 200). Quote exact. Full bracket: '[a position reminiscent of Dunnett's Francis Crawford of Lymond, whom Bertran resembles in many ways, especially in his skills as musician and military strategist]'. The page elsewhere names him 'the duke Bertran de Talair'. Note the sentence attaches 'reminiscent' first to Bertran's predicament (a hopeless search for his heir), then extends it to the man.

verdicts.trueWording: The colour symbolism of darkness and light has been retained
verdicts.note: Live fetch (HTTP 200). Quote exact, completed by 'in Arbonne's female characters'. The carried-from-Tigana limb is supported by the immediately preceding pages, which run the same dark/light scheme over Tigana's women (Catriana 'Red haired and associated with light', Eanna of the Lights vs the dark mother-goddess figures), and 'retained' is the essay's own word for the continuity.

verdicts.trueWording: GGK NOTE ... the source of my dissent from her reading
verdicts.note: Live fetch (HTTP 200). Quote exact. Kay's signed note ('- GGK') disputes Webb's gender reading directly: his dissent 'lies in the degree to which the text tries to make clear that it is an anomaly and a dangerous one that a woman is reigning in Arbonne', against her reading of the Blaise/Rinette marriage as a traditional union of male and female principles; 'unusual and generous step' supports the rarity limb. Placement detail: the note is interpolated mid-essay, immediately after the passage it answers, not at the very end.

verdicts.trueWording: She heard a crack, like a whip ... He would be scarred for life
verdicts.note: Live fetch (HTTP 200). Quote exact. Both limbs present: the Cronica source has the Cid 'pulled out part of his beard' from Garcia Ordonez, and Kay's scene has Belmonte's whip leave 'the black line of blood on Garcia de Rada's cheek'; Ordway: 'While pulling his beard was no doubt perceived as humiliating at the time of the Cid, it is unlikely to impress a modern reader, whereas the scarring does.' Page byline is 'by Holly E. Ordway May 13, 1998'; it carries no UMass Amherst or 1998 conference line, so that citation metadata is unconfirmed by this page (no claim limb depends on it).

verdicts.trueWording: By having the reconquest accomplished in only twenty years
verdicts.note: Live fetch (HTTP 200). Quote exact, and each limb: 'By having the reconquest accomplished in only twenty years, Kay has it occur in the lifetime of the characters ... The reader gets to experience the Jaddite victory through the perceptions of the characters who have ties to both sides, and so the complexities of the reconquest are brought home in a way that a simple epilogue or statement of the later victory could not.' The compression limb is backed by the contrast with the historical three hundred years.

verdicts.trueWording: he focuses on a single source for each novel
verdicts.note: Live fetch (HTTP 200). Quote exact, with the contrast term in the same sentence pair: 'In The Fionavar Tapestry, Kay draws on Tolkien as a main literary source, and on Norse and several other mythologies for further source material ... In his stand-alone novels ... but, in contrast, he focuses on a single source for each novel.'
